sections.title: The noise-driven iterates
sections.intro:
Given the initial vector \(x_0\) and innovations \(\xi_k\), define \(X_0=x_0\) and \(X_{k+1}=X_k-h\nabla U(X_k)+\sqrt{2h}\xi_k\). For fixed \(n\), the state depends only on the initial vector and \(\xi_0,\ldots,\xi_{n-1}\). The initial and successor identities follow from this definition.

If the initial vector and each innovation are measurable and the gradient is Lipschitz, every iterate is measurable by induction. The gradient is continuous, and measurable vector addition and scalar multiplication preserve the induction hypothesis. Gaussianity and independence are separate assumptions used when computing the laws of these iterates.

declarations.name: ulaChain
declarations.title: Definition of the chain
declarations.statement:
Given \(U:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\), \(h\in\mathbb R\), an initial vector \(x_0\), and noise \((\xi_k)\), define

\[X_0=x_0,\qquad X_{k+1}=X_k-h\nabla U(X_k)+\sqrt{2h}\,\xi_k.\]

steps.prose: Start the recursion at the supplied initial vector: \(X_0=x_0\).
steps.note:
Line 22. | 0 => initial

This is the first equation of ulaChain, not a tactic. The vertical bar begins a pattern-matching clause. The pattern 0 matches the final natural-number argument when it is zero. The symbol => separates that pattern from the returned value initial. Thus, after supplying U, h, initial, and noise, asking for index zero returns precisely the vector already named initial. The value has type E d, matching the announced output type. No equation needs to be proved to justify this clause: it defines the function's value. Lean checks that the clause has the correct type. The zero is a natural number because the argument being matched has type ℕ. This clause also provides the base of the recursive definition; evaluating it never calls ulaChain again.

The current task is to construct or identify an actual chain iterate. A local proof name denotes evidence of a stated property; a local function name denotes data. Any tactic must finish its current goal with a checked proof before Lean accepts the declaration.

steps.prose: Apply the Euler update to \(X_k\) using the next noise vector \(\xi_k\). This determines \(X_{k+1}\).
steps.note:
Line 23. | n + 1 => ulaUpdate U h (ulaChain U h initial noise n) (noise n)

The pattern n + 1 matches a successor index and gives its predecessor the local name n. This does not mean Lean searches arbitrary arithmetic decompositions: it is the natural-number successor pattern. To return the next vector, the right side applies ulaUpdate to four arguments: U, h, the current vector ulaChain U h initial noise n, and the next noise vector noise n. Spaces denote function application; the parentheses group the recursive call as one argument and the noise application as another. The recursive call uses n, smaller than the matched index n + 1, so Lean can verify that evaluation terminates. noise has type ℕ → E d, so noise n is a vector. No multiplication is implied by juxtaposing these names. The parameters U, h, initial, and noise remain fixed during recursion.

The current task is to construct or identify an actual chain iterate. A local proof name denotes evidence of a stated property; a local function name denotes data. Any tactic must finish its current goal with a checked proof before Lean accepts the declaration.

declarations.statement_note: def ulaChain introduces a function rather than a theorem. {d : ℕ} is an implicit natural-number dimension, usually inferred from the vector inputs. (U : E d → ℝ) is a real-valued potential, (h : ℝ) the step size, and (initial : E d) the starting vector. noise : ℕ → E d is a supplied sequence of vectors. The final : ℕ → E d says the result is itself a function of the iteration index. Thus ulaChain U h initial noise n returns one vector. The following pattern clauses give that function's values at zero and a successor. There are no assumptions here that the step is positive or that the noise is Gaussian; the recursion makes sense as a formal mathematical function before those extra properties are considered.

declarations.name: ulaChain_zero
declarations.title: The initial iterate
declarations.statement: For every potential, step, initial vector, and noise sequence, the recursively defined chain satisfies \(X_0=x_0\).

steps.prose: The equality is exactly the initial clause of the recursive definition.
steps.note:
Line 26. (initial : E d) (noise : ℕ → E d) : ulaChain U h initial noise 0 = initial := rfl

The continued header introduces two explicit inputs: initial : E d and noise : ℕ → E d. After the final colon comes the proposition to prove, ulaChain U h initial noise 0 = initial. Here = is a mathematical equality, while := separates the theorem statement from its proof. The proof is rfl, short for reflexivity. Lean evaluates the zero clause of ulaChain; both sides then become the same vector initial, so reflexivity proves the equality. The theorem is not assuming the equality. It supplies a checked proof of it for every listed input. The preceding attribute @[simp] registers this theorem as a simplification rule, so a later simp can replace an initial-chain expression by initial. Although rfl often appears inside a by block, it can also be used directly as the proof term shown here.

The current task is to construct or identify an actual chain iterate. A local proof name denotes evidence of a stated property; a local function name denotes data. Any tactic must finish its current goal with a checked proof before Lean accepts the declaration.

declarations.statement_note: This theorem states a proposition and supplies a proof. It has the same dimension, potential, step, starting vector, and noise parameters as ulaChain. The dimension uses braces because Lean can infer it from the typed vector arguments; parentheses introduce explicit arguments. The proposition after the final colon is equality of the zero-th iterate with initial. In the continued header, := rfl is the proof, not part of the claimed equality. The attribute @[simp] tells Lean that this proved equation is suitable for automatic simplification. It does not add a hypothesis or assume the statement. This theorem is universally reusable for all supplied parameters, and its proof needs no conditions on the measure, step size, or noise because the equality follows from the chain's defining zero clause.

declarations.name: ulaChain_succ
declarations.title: The update identity
declarations.statement: For every \(k\ge0\), the chain satisfies \(X_{k+1}=T_h^{\xi_k}(X_k)\).

steps.prose: The successor clause of the recursion gives the asserted update formula.
steps.note:
Line 31. ulaUpdate U h (ulaChain U h initial noise n) (noise n) := rfl

This line completes the right-hand side of the equality begun in the preceding header. ulaUpdate U h receives the vector at time n and the noise at time n. The enclosing theorem claims that this equals the chain at time n + 1. The symbol := starts the proof, and rfl checks it by reducing the successor clause of the recursive definition. A line break does not end a Lean expression: the indentation continues the statement until :=. The equality is true by the definition of this particular chain, without requiring positivity of h, measurability, Gaussian noise, or a Lipschitz bound. Those are separate mathematical questions. The @[simp] attribute on the theorem makes this update equation available to the simplifier; the proof below explicitly chooses it in simp only [ulaChain_succ, ulaUpdate].

The current task is to construct or identify an actual chain iterate. A local proof name denotes evidence of a stated property; a local function name denotes data. Any tactic must finish its current goal with a checked proof before Lean accepts the declaration.

declarations.statement_note: The inputs are the same data used to define the chain, plus n : ℕ, an explicit natural index. The dimension d remains implicit and is inferred from initial or U. The equality following the final colon identifies the iterate at n + 1 with one update of the iterate at n, using noise n. A function application such as noise n supplies an index to a sequence; it is not multiplication. The long equation is split across lines for readability, and its proof begins only at :=. The @[simp] attribute registers the update equation for the simplifier. Proving this equation requires only the recursive definition, so no contraction, measurability, or stochastic-noise assumptions occur in the header.

declarations.name: ulaChain_measurable
declarations.title: Measurability of every iterate
declarations.statement: Let \(\Omega\) be a measurable space. If \(\nabla U\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz, the initial vector \(X_0:\Omega\to\mathbb R^d\) is measurable, and every \(\xi_k:\Omega\to\mathbb R^d\) is measurable, then \(X_n\) is measurable for every \(n\).

steps.prose: A Lipschitz gradient is continuous and therefore measurable.
steps.note:
Line 40. have hg : Measurable (gradient U) := hLip.continuous.measurable

have hg : Measurable (gradient U) := ... adds a local proved fact called hg. Before the colon is its chosen name; after the colon is its proposition; after := is the proof supplied. The existing hypothesis hLip proves that gradient U is L-Lipschitz. Dot notation hLip.continuous applies the library theorem saying that a Lipschitz map is continuous. The next .measurable applies the theorem saying a continuous map between these Borel spaces is measurable. Thus this expression successively turns one proof into another. gradient U is a function, and Measurable is a property of that function; hg is a proof, not a new gradient value. Establishing hg does not finish the main goal of measurability of the whole chain. It stores a reusable ingredient for the successor case. The type of hg makes clear exactly which function is measurable.

The current task is to construct or identify an actual chain iterate. A local proof name denotes evidence of a stated property; a local function name denotes data. Any tactic must finish its current goal with a checked proof before Lean accepts the declaration.

steps.prose: Induct on \(n\). The initial iterate is measurable by hypothesis. For the successor step, assume \(X_n\) is measurable.
steps.note:
Line 41. induction n with

induction n with replaces the goal “the iterate at every specified index n is measurable” by the two cases of natural-number induction. One must prove it at index zero and prove it at a successor assuming it at the predecessor. with introduces the following named branches.

Line 42. | zero => exact hinitial

The branch marker | zero => selects index zero. The chain reduces to initial, so the current goal becomes Measurable initial. exact hinitial closes that goal using the hypothesis of exactly that type. exact does not assert an unproved fact: it asks Lean to check that the supplied proof has the goal's type.

Line 43. | succ n ih =>

The successor branch introduces a predecessor named n and an induction hypothesis named ih. Here ih proves measurability of the function sending ω to the chain at index n. The remaining goal is measurability of the chain at index n + 1. The following indented lines belong to this branch. These names are local to it; ih is not a Lean keyword and could have been called hprevious.

The current task is to construct or identify an actual chain iterate. A local proof name denotes evidence of a stated property; a local function name denotes data. Any tactic must finish its current goal with a checked proof before Lean accepts the declaration.

steps.prose: The composition \(\nabla U\circ X_n\) is measurable. Subtracting its scalar multiple from \(X_n\), then adding \(\sqrt{2h}\,\xi_n\), preserves measurability. Hence \(X_{n+1}\) is measurable.
steps.note:
Line 44. simp only [ulaChain_succ, ulaUpdate]

simp only [ulaChain_succ, ulaUpdate] unfolds the successor iterate and the formula for one update in the goal. The brackets list exactly the additional named rules/definitions to use; they are not a list of chain values. only keeps the simplifier from using the full ambient collection of simp lemmas. The resulting function is the current iterate minus its drift plus its scaled noise.

Line 45. exact (ih.sub ((hg.comp ih).const_smul h)).add

exact begins one proof expression, continued on the next line. hg.comp ih proves measurability of the gradient composed with the current iterate. .const_smul h proves measurability after multiplication of its vector values by the fixed scalar h. Then ih.sub ... proves measurability of the difference. Finally .add requests a measurable second summand, supplied by the next line. Parentheses group the intermediate proof objects; these methods are theorems about measurability, not subtraction or addition of proofs.

Line 46. ((hnoise n).const_smul (Real.sqrt (2 * h)))

hnoise n specializes the assumption of measurable noise to this index. Its .const_smul (Real.sqrt (2 * h)) consequence proves that the scaled noise is measurable. This is passed to the unfinished .add on line 45, completing measurability of the update and closing the successor case. Real.sqrt is the real square-root function; the nested parentheses keep its whole value together as the scalar argument. No independence assumption is needed for this measurable-function calculation.

declarations.statement_note: {Ω : Type*} introduces an inferred sample type and [MeasurableSpace Ω] asks Lean to supply its measurable-set structure. {d : ℕ} is the inferred vector dimension. The explicit data are U, h, the finite nonnegative Lipschitz constant L, a sample-dependent initial vector, a time-and-sample-dependent noise family, and the final index n. The hypotheses hLip, hinitial, and hnoise are proofs, respectively, of a Lipschitz gradient, initial measurability, and measurability of every noise vector. The final conclusion is measurability of the sample-to-vector function defined by the actual chain at time n. The inner lambda fixes a sample to obtain the deterministic noise sequence required by ulaChain. This theorem proves a function property, without introducing a probability law or an independence assumption.

sections.title: Couplings and quadratic transport
sections.intro:
Let \(H\) be a second-countable normed space with its Borel sigma-algebra. A coupling of \(\mu, u\) is a measure \(\gamma\) on \(H imes H\) with those marginals. Set \(c(\gamma)=(\int\|x-y\|^2d\gamma)^{1/2}\) and \(W_2(\mu, u)=\inf_{\gamma\in\Gamma(\mu, u)}c(\gamma)\), with extended nonnegative values allowed. A coupling with finite cost proves that this transport infimum is finite.

For measurable random vectors on the same probability space, the joint law is a coupling of their marginal laws, and its cost equals \(\|X-Y\|_2\). Consequently an estimate of the mean-square difference bounds the transport distance. The same statements hold for almost-everywhere measurable representatives. Pointwise domination, Minkowski, and finite second moments give the one-step error estimates below; independence of the compared variables is not required.

declarations.name: Coupling
declarations.title: Definition of a coupling
declarations.statement: A coupling of measures \(\mu,\nu\) on \(H\) is a joint measure \(\gamma\) on \(H\times H\) with those two marginals. Denote the family by \(\Gamma(\mu,\nu)\).

steps.prose: Choose the joint measure \(\gamma\) on pairs \((x,y)\).
steps.note:
Line 32. joint : Measure (H × H)

This line declares a field of the new structure Coupling μ ν. A structure is a record bundling several pieces of data and proofs. The field's name is joint, and its type is Measure (H × H), a measure on ordered pairs of elements of H. The colon announces a type; there is no := because no specific joint measure is being chosen in the definition of the record type. Instead, anyone constructing a coupling must later supply a measure for this field. × forms the product type, not multiplication of numbers. An element can be written (x, y). The field can later be accessed as c.joint for a coupling c. The declaration introduces the shape of admissible data; the following two fields impose the marginal obligations on whatever measure is supplied.

Throughout this argument, laws are pushforward measures and the extended seminorm may be infinite unless a finite-moment hypothesis is supplied. Keep the mathematical function separate from the proof that it is measurable: both are arguments in Lean, but they have different types and roles.

steps.prose: Require \((\operatorname{pr}_1)_\#\gamma=\mu\) and \((\operatorname{pr}_2)_\#\gamma=\nu\).
steps.note:
Line 33. fst : joint.map Prod.fst = μ

The field fst has a proposition as its type: joint.map Prod.fst = μ. Therefore its value must be a proof of that equality. Prod.fst is the function taking a pair to its first coordinate. joint.map Prod.fst is the pushforward measure, the first marginal of joint. The already declared joint field can be used in the type of a later field. This records a dependency: a proof about that particular joint measure is required.

Line 34. snd : joint.map Prod.snd = ν

The field snd similarly requires a proof that the second-coordinate pushforward is ν. Prod.snd is the second projection. These field names do not themselves compute the marginals; they name the proofs that the marginals have the required values. A completed coupling therefore contains one measure and two checked equality proofs. The notation c.fst retrieves its first marginal proof, while c.snd retrieves the second.

Throughout this argument, laws are pushforward measures and the extended seminorm may be infinite unless a finite-moment hypothesis is supplied. Keep the mathematical function separate from the proof that it is measurable: both are arguments in Lean, but they have different types and roles.

declarations.statement_note: structure Coupling (μ ν : Measure H) where defines a new record type depending on two explicit measures. It inherits the ambient type H and whichever declared structures its fields require; the two measures determine the intended marginals. A value c : Coupling μ ν must contain all three fields listed below: one joint measure and two proofs of marginal equalities. The word where opens the field declarations. A field ending in : Measure ... stores mathematical data, while a field whose type is an equality stores a proof. This is how the formalization makes admissibility part of a coupling's type. A bare joint measure is not automatically a coupling. Later c.joint retrieves its measure, while c.fst and c.snd retrieve the certified marginal identities.

declarations.name: couplingCost
declarations.title: Definition of quadratic coupling cost
declarations.statement:
For a joint measure \(\gamma\), define

\[c(\gamma)=\left(\int\|x-y\|^2\,d\gamma(x,y)\right)^{1/2}\in[0,+\infty].\]

steps.prose: Take the extended \(L^2(\gamma)\) norm of the displacement map \((x,y)\mapsto x-y\).
steps.note:
Line 38. eLpNorm (fun p : H × H ↦ p.1 - p.2) 2 γ

This is the value assigned to couplingCost γ after the preceding header's :=. eLpNorm receives three visible arguments: the displacement function, exponent 2, and measure γ. The expression fun p : H × H ↦ p.1 - p.2 creates a function: give its input the name p and return the first component minus the second. The explicit type annotation tells Lean that p is a pair; p.1 and p.2 retrieve its coordinates. ↦ separates function arguments from the returned expression. This is a lambda expression, not a logical implication. The result of eLpNorm lies in ℝ≥0∞, permitting an infinite second moment. Thus this definition does not first assert integrability or convert infinity to a real number. The exponent 2 makes the seminorm the square root of the second moment.

Throughout this argument, laws are pushforward measures and the extended seminorm may be infinite unless a finite-moment hypothesis is supplied. Keep the mathematical function separate from the proof that it is measurable: both are arguments in Lean, but they have different types and roles.

declarations.statement_note: The header def couplingCost (γ : Measure (H × H)) : ℝ≥0∞ := defines a value from one explicit joint measure. The ambient normed-group structure on H supplies subtraction and norm. H × H is a product type, so γ measures pairs rather than individual vectors. The result type ℝ≥0∞ permits both finite nonnegative costs and positive infinity. Its definition uses an extended seminorm of the displacement, with exponent two. Because this takes any joint measure, the header does not require marginal proofs or take a Coupling record. Those constraints become relevant when minimizing over couplings. := introduces the actual defining expression below; a definition needs a correctly typed expression rather than a tactic proof of a proposition.

declarations.name: wasserstein2
declarations.title: Definition of the transport infimum
declarations.statement:
Define the extended quadratic transport distance by

\[W_2(\mu,\nu)=\inf_{\gamma\in\Gamma(\mu,\nu)}c(\gamma).\]

steps.prose: Take the infimum over all couplings without selecting a minimizer.
steps.note:
Line 42. ⨅ c : Coupling μ ν, couplingCost c.joint

The symbol ⨅ forms an indexed infimum. Its bound variable is c, whose type is Coupling μ ν; the comma separates that binder from the expression whose infimum is taken. For every such record, c.joint extracts its joint measure, and couplingCost c.joint assigns its extended cost. The infimum of these costs is the definition of wasserstein2 μ ν. It lies in ℝ≥0∞, whose order admits infima even when there are no couplings: the infimum of an empty family is then ⊤. No particular minimizing c is chosen, and the definition does not claim one exists. The type annotation after c : is especially useful here: the index ranges over complete coupling records, including their marginal proofs, rather than over arbitrary joint measures. See the notation guide for entering mathematical symbols.

Throughout this argument, laws are pushforward measures and the extended seminorm may be infinite unless a finite-moment hypothesis is supplied. Keep the mathematical function separate from the proof that it is measurable: both are arguments in Lean, but they have different types and roles.

declarations.statement_note: def wasserstein2 (μ ν : Measure H) : ℝ≥0∞ := introduces the extended distance as a function of two measures. The ambient type H, subtraction, norm, and measurable structure are inferred from those measures and the available instances. The result lives in the extended nonnegative reals, so the definition can represent an infinite transport cost rather than forcing every value into ℝ. The expression below ranges over the type Coupling μ ν; each possible index already contains both marginal proofs. The declaration does not assume that this type is nonempty or that its infimum is attained. Order completeness gives an infimum even for an empty family, whose value is then infinity. The name ending in 2 identifies the quadratic cost defined above, not an exponent automatically attached to the output.

declarations.name: wasserstein2Real
declarations.title: Finite quadratic Wasserstein distance
declarations.statement: The infimum defining quadratic Wasserstein distance takes values in \([0,\infty]\). Whenever it is finite, it can be used as an ordinary nonnegative real number. Each estimate below proves finiteness from a finite coupling cost before performing real arithmetic with the distance.

steps.prose: Restrict attention to a pair of measures with finite quadratic Wasserstein distance. Its finite value has the same order comparisons as the extended nonnegative value. Thus the previously proved coupling inequalities apply as inequalities between real numbers.
steps.note:
Line 46. def wasserstein2Real (μ ν : Measure H) : ℝ := (wasserstein2 μ ν).toReal

def introduces a named mathematical definition. (μ ν : Measure H) is short for two explicit parameters of the same type. The final : ℝ states that the result is a real number, and := gives its defining value. First wasserstein2 μ ν computes the extended nonnegative-real distance; then .toReal converts it to a real. The parentheses make that whole distance the receiver of the conversion. The conversion returns the ordinary value when the argument is finite, but sends ⊤ to 0. Therefore this definition alone does not justify interpreting it as a finite transport distance for all measures. The later comparison lemmas supply finite bounds before transporting inequalities through toReal. This line defines a value rather than proving a theorem, so there is no pending goal or tactic block. Lean still checks that the right side has type ℝ.

Throughout this argument, laws are pushforward measures and the extended seminorm may be infinite unless a finite-moment hypothesis is supplied. Keep the mathematical function separate from the proof that it is measurable: both are arguments in Lean, but they have different types and roles.

declarations.statement_note: This definition takes the same two measures as wasserstein2, but declares a real-valued output : ℝ. It inherits the ambient vector and measurable structures needed to form the extended transport distance. Its body applies toReal to that extended value. The name Real in the identifier is explanatory; Lean determines the output type from the type annotation and body. Since toReal maps infinity to zero, finite-distance hypotheses must accompany later mathematical uses of this conversion. This declaration is not itself a theorem that the distance is finite. A caller supplies measures as wasserstein2Real μ ν, using spaces for function application. The equality sign inside a later theorem will state a claim about that value, whereas the := here specifies how the value is defined.

declarations.name: wasserstein2_le_couplingCost
declarations.title: Every coupling supplies an upper bound
declarations.statement: For every \(\gamma\in\Gamma(\mu,\nu)\), \(W_2(\mu,\nu)\le c(\gamma)\).

steps.prose: An infimum is at most each member of the family. Apply this to the chosen coupling.
steps.note:
Line 52. iInf_le _ c

This is a complete proof term for the inequality in the header. The library theorem iInf_le says that an indexed infimum is at most the value at any chosen index. Its first explicit argument is the indexed family of costs; _ asks Lean to infer that family from the expected conclusion. Its second argument is c, the particular coupling supplied to this theorem. Lean unfolds enough of wasserstein2 to recognize that its index family is fun c ↦ couplingCost c.joint. The resulting inequality is precisely wasserstein2 μ ν ≤ couplingCost c.joint. An underscore is a request for an inferable expression, not an unproved mathematical gap; the finished declaration is accepted only after it is filled. Because the whole proof is one term, the header uses := followed by that term instead of opening a by tactic block.

Throughout this argument, laws are pushforward measures and the extended seminorm may be infinite unless a finite-moment hypothesis is supplied. Keep the mathematical function separate from the proof that it is measurable: both are arguments in Lean, but they have different types and roles.

declarations.statement_note: The measures {μ ν : Measure H} are implicit parameters, inferable from the explicit coupling c : Coupling μ ν. The ambient H and required instances are inherited from the section. After the colon, the theorem claims that the infimum transport value is at most couplingCost c.joint. The dot access extracts the joint measure from this admissible coupling record. Both sides have extended nonnegative-real type, so no finiteness assumption is needed. The theorem returns a proof of this inequality for each supplied coupling; it does not select a new coupling or calculate an optimal one. Its body is the short proof term iInf_le _ c, supplied directly after :=. The underscore will be inferred from the target family of costs rather than left as an unresolved gap.

declarations.name: randomVariableCoupling
declarations.title: The joint law of two random vectors
declarations.statement: If \(X,Y:\Omega\to H\) are measurable, then \((X,Y)_\#P\) is a coupling of \(X_\#P\) and \(Y_\#P\).

steps.prose: Set \(\gamma=(\omega\mapsto(X(\omega),Y(\omega)))_\#P\).
steps.note:
Line 59. joint := P.map (fun ω ↦ (X ω, Y ω))

In the where block constructing a Coupling, joint := ... fills the data field called joint. The assigned measure is P.map (fun ω ↦ (X ω, Y ω)), the joint law of the two functions on the same sample space. The lambda takes one sample ω and returns the pair of vectors at that sample. P.map is pushforward, not an array operation. Here := assigns a record field its value; it does not prove the marginal equations by itself. The construction must still provide fst and snd proofs, as the following fields do. The hypotheses hX and hY are proofs that the paired map has the needed measurability. Keeping the same ω in both coordinates is what constructs a coupling of these particular jointly realized vectors.

Throughout this argument, laws are pushforward measures and the extended seminorm may be infinite unless a finite-moment hypothesis is supplied. Keep the mathematical function separate from the proof that it is measurable: both are arguments in Lean, but they have different types and roles.

steps.prose: Compose the pushforward with the first projection. Since \(\operatorname{pr}_1(X(\omega),Y(\omega))=X(\omega)\), the first marginal is \(X_\#P\).
steps.note:
Line 60. fst := by

fst := by fills the coupling's first marginal proof. The field's type supplies the current goal: pushing the chosen joint measure forward along Prod.fst must yield P.map X. by begins a tactic proof local to this field; the indented lines are its proof commands.

Line 61. rw [Measure.map_map measurable_fst (hX.prodMk hY)]

rw [...] rewrites that goal using Measure.map_map, which combines two successive pushforwards into a pushforward under composition. Its explicit proof arguments are measurable_fst, measurability of the projection, and hX.prodMk hY, measurability of the paired map. Dot notation .prodMk applies the library pairing theorem to the two measurability proofs. Brackets here contain rewrite rules to apply, not typeclass instances.

Line 62. rfl

rfl closes the rewritten goal. Projecting the first coordinate of (X ω, Y ω) evaluates to X ω, so the composed function is definitionally the original X. Lean can reduce this computation without a further measure theorem. The proof concerns the equality of measures after that function has reduced; it is not asserting that arbitrary measures are reflexively equal.

Throughout this argument, laws are pushforward measures and the extended seminorm may be infinite unless a finite-moment hypothesis is supplied. Keep the mathematical function separate from the proof that it is measurable: both are arguments in Lean, but they have different types and roles.

steps.prose: The same calculation with the second projection gives the second marginal \(Y_\#P\).
steps.note:
Line 63. snd := by

snd := by opens the proof required for the second marginal field of this same record. Its current goal is the equality between the second-coordinate pushforward of the joint law and P.map Y. The previously chosen joint value is fixed; the field proof verifies a property of it.

Line 64. rw [Measure.map_map measurable_snd (hX.prodMk hY)]

The rewrite again uses Measure.map_map, now with measurable_snd proving measurability of the second projection. hX.prodMk hY proves measurability of the same paired random vector. The theorem turns the two maps into a single map under the composition “form the pair, then take its second coordinate.” rw changes the goal by a proved equality, preserving what must be established.

Line 65. rfl

rfl finishes because the second coordinate of (X ω, Y ω) reduces to Y ω. This completes the last record field, so Lean now has a full value of type Coupling (P.map X) (P.map Y). The two marginal proofs are separate fields because satisfying one marginal constraint alone would not make the joint measure a coupling of both specified laws.

declarations.name: wasserstein2_le_Lp_cost
declarations.title: The transport bound for L² classes
declarations.statement:
For \(X,Y\in L^2(P;H)\), their representatives define laws satisfying

\[W_2(X_\#P,Y_\#P)\le\|X-Y\|_{L^2}.\]

declarations.name: synchronous_l2_bound
declarations.title: One-step error from contraction and a defect
declarations.statement:
Suppose \(q\ge0\), \(A\) is almost everywhere strongly measurable, and almost everywhere

\[X'-Y'=A-V,\qquad\|A\|\le q\|X-Y\|.\]

Then

\[\|X'-Y'\|_{2,P}\le q\|X-Y\|_{2,P}+\|V\|_{2,P}.\]

steps.prose: Replace \(X'-Y'\) by \(A-V\) in the seminorm using the almost everywhere error identity.
steps.note:

rw [eLpNorm_congr_ae hidentity] rewrites the extended norm of the next-step displacement using the supplied almost everywhere identity hidentity. The theorem eLpNorm_congr_ae says that functions equal almost everywhere have the same extended seminorm. Here the functions are ω ↦ X' ω - Y' ω and ω ↦ A ω - V ω. Although the hypothesis is written as ∀ᵐ ω ∂P, ..., that is exactly the pointwise almost everywhere equality the theorem needs. Brackets pass the resulting equality proof to the rewriting tactic. The main goal becomes a bound for the norm of A - V, which is now ready for the triangle inequality. This does not replace the functions pointwise on the exceptional set; it uses the fact that the integral-based seminorm ignores differences on null sets.

eLpNorm_sub_le gives the extended-norm triangle inequality for a difference. It requires the exponent to be at least one; (by norm_num : (1 : ℝ≥0∞) ≤ 2) is an inline proof with an explicit proposition, checked by numerical normalization. Appending .trans will compose this inequality with the bound supplied on the next line.

add_le_add combines two inequalities between summands. The first is eLpNorm_contraction P A (fun ω ↦ X ω - Y ω) q hA hcontract, bounding the A term. sections.title: Propagation of finite error moments
sections.intro:
Suppose \(E=A-V\) almost everywhere, \(A\) is almost everywhere strongly measurable, and \(\|A\|\le q\|D\|\). Finite \(L^p\) membership of \(D\) transfers to \(A\) by domination, and finite \(L^p\) membership of \(V\) then gives that of \(E\). Applied to successive coupled Euler updates, this proves finite second moments of every error from the finite initial error and finite defects.

The common noise cancels in the difference of the updates. Hence the moment induction uses only the preceding error and the defect. A contraction factor strictly below one is not needed for this finiteness result; that restriction is imposed when summing the convergence recurrence.

declarations.name: synchronous_memLp

have hAmem : MemLp A p P := ... creates a local proof that A has the required finite Lp moment. hD already proves MemLp D p P. Its method .of_le_mul hA hcontract applies the domination theorem: the almost everywhere strongly measurable function A, with proof hA, has its pointwise norm bounded by the constant multiple of D stated in hcontract. This passes finite Lp membership from D to A. The supplied exponent is the arbitrary header parameter p, not necessarily two. The theorem also has a real coefficient q; no separate nonnegative coefficient premise is needed for this membership transfer, because the assumed norm bound is already enough. The conclusion is a proposition and hAmem stores its proof, so this line does not define a new function A.

sections.title: Iteration of the scalar error estimate
sections.intro:
Let a real sequence satisfy \(e_{k+1}\le qe_k+b\), with \(q\ge0\). Induction gives \(e_n\le q^ne_0+b\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}q^j\). If \(0\le q<1\), the sum equals \((1-q^n)/(1-q)\). When \(b\ge0\), it is bounded by \(1/(1-q)\), giving a uniform additive bound \(b/(1-q)\).

The upper-bound sequence \(q^ne_0+b/(1-q)\) converges to \(b/(1-q)\). Therefore every tolerance strictly above this value eventually bounds the errors. This conclusion does not imply that the error sequence itself converges or has this limit.

declarations.name: affine_recurrence_sum
declarations.title: Iteration gives a geometric sum
declarations.statement:
If \(q\ge0\) and \(e_{k+1}\le qe_k+b\) for every \(k\), then

\[e_n\le q^ne_0+b\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}q^j.\]

steps.prose: Induct on \(n\). At zero the sum is empty and both sides equal \(e_0\). Assume the bound at \(n\).

Line 23. induction n with

induction n with proves the finite-sum estimate by natural-number induction. The sequence e, coefficient q, defect bound b, and one-step hypothesis hstep stay fixed. Lean produces a goal at index zero and a successor goal in which the predecessor estimate may be assumed.

| zero => simp handles index zero. The simplifier reduces q ^ 0 to 1, the sum over Finset.range 0 to 0, and the surrounding arithmetic to the reflexive inequality e 0 ≤ e 0. Those are previously proved simp facts and definitional computations, not a new estimate for the sequence.

Line 25. | succ n ih =>

The successor branch introduces the predecessor index n and a proof ih of the bound at that index. The goal is the same bound at n + 1. Function application uses a space, so e 0 is the initial value. q ^ n is exponentiation; * is multiplication. ∀ n, ... means “for every natural-number index,” with the type inferred from its use in e.

sections.title: Passing from a chosen initial coupling to an infimum
sections.intro:
Let the output measures be fixed and assume that every initial coupling gives an affine bound in its cost with the same constants. Taking the infimum over couplings gives the corresponding bound in \(W_2(\mu,\nu)\). This uses the infimum property and does not assume an optimal coupling.

If the initial transport distance is finite, a finite-cost coupling exists. Approximate minimizing couplings then suffice even if the assumed estimate is stated only for finite-cost couplings. When the affine coefficient is zero, one such coupling already proves the constant bound. When it is positive, couplings with cost approaching the infimum give the result by taking a limit.

declarations.name: wasserstein2_affine_bound_of_all_couplings
declarations.title: A uniform affine estimate passes to the infimum
declarations.statement:
Let \(a\ge0\) be finite, \(b\in[0,+\infty]\), and \(\Gamma(\mu, u) e\varnothing\). If the fixed output measures satisfy

\[W_2(\mu', u')\le ac(\gamma)+b\quad ext{for every }\gamma\in\Gamma(\mu, u),\]

then \(W_2(\mu', u')\le aW_2(\mu, u)+b\).

steps.prose: Use the nonempty coupling family and expand transport distances as infima.
steps.note:
Line 31. let : Nonempty (Coupling μ ν) := hnonempty

let : Nonempty (Coupling μ ν) := hnonempty installs the supplied nonemptiness proof as an anonymous local instance. There is no identifier between let and the colon: later library code finds this proof by its type through instance search. The type Nonempty (Coupling μ ν) says an initial coupling exists. This special use of let introduces instance data rather than a named numerical abbreviation. It does not choose a specific optimal coupling.

Line 32. unfold wasserstein2

unfold wasserstein2 expands the definition of the transport infima in the goal. The right side contains the infimum over initial coupling costs and the left side the infimum over output coupling costs. Opening the definition exposes the ⨅ notation so the next infimum identities can apply. The mathematical hypotheses, including the uniform bound hfamily, remain available under their existing names.

The initial couplings may vary, while the output laws remain fixed. All conversions between finite, extended, and real numbers must match their types. In particular, toReal requires finite upper bounds when used to preserve an inequality in this argument.

steps.prose: Multiplication by finite \(a\ge0\) and addition of \(b\) commute with the nonempty extended-real infimum, including \(a=0\). Thus \(aW_2(\mu,\nu)+b=\inf_\gamma(ac(\gamma)+b)\).

rw rewrites the goal using two extended-real infimum identities. ENNReal.mul_iInf moves multiplication by the finite coefficient across the indexed infimum, and ENNReal.iInf_add moves addition of b across it. The first theorem receives fun h ↦ (ENNReal.coe_ne_top h).elim, a proof that the troublesome infinite-coefficient case is impossible. In that lambda, h is a hypothetical equality making the embedded finite coefficient equal to ⊤. ENNReal.coe_ne_top h produces a contradiction; .elim uses the impossibility to prove the required exceptional-case condition. This does not posit that a finite coefficient is infinite. The nonempty instance installed on line 31 supplies the condition needed for the infimum/addition manipulation. The result is an infimum of the affine cost expression to which hfamily applies pointwise, including the case of zero coefficient.

The initial couplings may vary, while the output laws remain fixed. All conversions between finite, extended, and real numbers must match their types. In particular, toReal requires finite upper bounds when used to preserve an inequality in this argument.

Its argument hfamily is already a function taking an initial coupling c to the desired bound by that coupling's affine cost. Thus Lean does not need an explicit intro c here: the proof function is supplied directly. exact checks that, after the preceding rewrites, this conclusion matches the goal and closes it. This theorem contrasts with iInf_le used earlier: iInf_le bounds an infimum above by one member, while le_iInf bounds it below using all members. The uniformity in hfamily is therefore essential. declarations.title: The real uniform-coupling estimate
declarations.statement:
Let \(a,b\ge0\) be finite and assume \(W_2(\mu, u)<+\infty\). If \(W_2(\mu', u')\le ac(\gamma)+b\) for every initial coupling, then

\[W_2(\mu', u')\le aW_2(\mu, u)+b.\]

declarations.statement:
Let \(a,b\ge0\) be finite. Assume both the initial and output transport distances are finite and that every finite-cost \(\gamma\in\Gamma(\mu, u)\) satisfies

\[W_2(\mu', u')\le ac(\gamma)+b.\]

Then \(W_2(\mu', u')\le aW_2(\mu, u)+b\).

Ambient names and types. Importing UnadjustedLangevin.Coupling makes the coupling structure and extended and real transport distances available. open MeasureTheory shortens measure-theoretic names, and open scoped NNReal ENNReal enables ℝ≥0 and ℝ≥0∞. noncomputable section allows definitions based on nonalgorithmic mathematical operations; the proofs remain checked. namespace ULA places the new theorems alongside the previously defined objects.

Braces make the type implicit, and square brackets request the named structures by typeclass search. Each theorem explicitly introduces its measures. (μ ν μ' ν' : Measure H) declares four separate measures of the same type; the apostrophes are simply part of the names and do not denote derivatives here.

sections.title: The conditional common-noise convergence theorem
sections.intro:
Let \(X_k\) be the numerical iterates and \(Y_k\) a supplied reference on the same probability space, with \(\mathcal L(Y_k)=\pi\). Assume a common-noise update contraction with factor \(0\le q<1\), a finite initial mean-square difference, and square-integrable reference defects bounded in norm by \(b\). Subtracting the updates gives \(e_{k+1}\le qe_k+b\), where \(e_k=\|X_k-Y_k\|_2\). Moment propagation ensures these norms are finite.

The joint law of \((X_n,Y_n)\) bounds \(W_2(\mathcal L(X_n),\pi)\) by \(e_n\). Iteration gives the stated transport estimate. Its initial term is the cost of the supplied coupling. Replacing that cost by an initial Wasserstein distance requires the same construction and constants for every finite-cost initial coupling.

declarations.name: ula_wasserstein_bound_of_reference
declarations.title: Transport bound from a supplied discrete reference
declarations.statement:
Let \(\nabla U\) be \(L\)-Lipschitz, \(0\le q<1\), and \(b\ge0\). Assume the initial vector, all noise vectors, and all reference vectors \(Y_k\) are measurable; \((Y_k)_\#P=\pi\); and

\[Y_{k+1}=T_h^{\xi_k}(Y_k)+V_k\quad\text{almost everywhere}.\]

Suppose the common-noise update is \(q\)-contractive, \(X_0-Y_0\in L^2\), every \(V_k\in L^2\), and \(\|V_k\|_2\le b\). Then

\[W_2((X_n)_\#P,\pi)\le q^n\|X_0-Y_0\|_2+\frac b{1-q}.\]

The initial term is the cost of the chosen coupled pair.

The following membership results establish that these converted seminorms are finite norms rather than converted infinities.

sections.title: Convergence in a Hilbert space of random variables
sections.intro:
Let \(\mathcal H=L^2(P;H)\) and let the gradient act by pointwise composition. Supply continuous reference segments \(Y_{k,t}\), joining at grid endpoints, whose grid laws equal \(\pi\). Their endpoint noise is the innovation driving the numerical step. The reference integral equation and the bounds \(\|g(Y_{k,t})\|_2\le\sqrt{Ld}\) and \(\|B_{k,t}\|_2\le\sqrt{2d}\sqrt t\) give a defect norm at most \((33/20)Lh\sqrt{hd}\) when \(Lh\le2\).

The common-noise subtraction and the deterministic Euler contraction give an affine recurrence in \(\mathcal H\). Its geometric sum bounds the transport distance of the numerical law from \(\pi\). The two step ranges use factors \(1-mh\) and \(Lh-1\), respectively. The reference and its stationary laws are hypotheses here; the Brownian construction later supplies them.

\[W_2((X_n)_\#P,\pi)\le q^n\|X_0-Y_{0,0}\|_2+\frac{(33/20)Lh\sqrt{hd}}{1-q}.\]
